citations.title: What is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)?
citations.excerpt:
Summary:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances large language models by first retrieving relevant, authoritative external documents from knowledge sources (e.g., policy manuals, databases) and then supplying those retrieved materials to the LLM as context. This approach keeps outputs accurate and up-to-date without retraining the model, improves domain-specific or organization-specific responses, and provides transparency by showing the sourcing process. The workflow typically involves: converting the user query into a vector, retrieving highly relevant documents from vector databases, and augmenting the prompt with this retrieved data before the LLM generates a response. This enables precise, context-aware answers (e.g., HR policies, technical docs) while maintaining control over content quality.

citations.title: RAG and Generative AI - Azure AI Search | Microsoft Learn
citations.excerpt:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in Azure AI Search is a pattern that grounds LLM outputs in your own content. Microsoft Learn distinguishes two approaches:

- Agentic retrieval (preview): A complete RAG pipeline that uses LLM-assisted query planning, multi-source access, parallel subqueries, and structured, grounded responses optimized for chat. Features include context-aware query planning, parallel subqueries, structured results with citations and execution metadata, built-in semantic ranking, and optional LLM-synthesized answers. Recommended for new RAG implementations.
- Classic RAG: The traditional approach using a single user query to Azure AI Search, then an LLM synthesizes an answer from the flattened results. Simpler to implement, fewer components, and faster when GA features are required or query planning isn’t needed.

Key takeaway: For authoritative, technically grounded RAG implementations, agentic retrieval is the modern, recommended pattern, offering better accuracy and context handling through multi-query, structured, and cited responses. Classic RAG remains suitable for simpler or GA-only use cases.

citations.title: Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and indexes in Microsoft Foundry - Microsoft Foundry | Microsoft Learn
citations.excerpt:
Summary:
This Microsoft Learn article defines and explains Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) in Microsoft Foundry. RAG combines search with large language models to ground responses in your data, using an index to retrieve relevant content, and then augmenting prompts before generation. Key concepts:
- Grounding data: retrieved content provided to the model to reduce guessing and enable citations.
- Index: data structure for efficient retrieval (keyword, semantic, vector, or hybrid search). 
- Embeddings: numeric representations used for vector similarity search.
- RAG workflow (three steps): Retrieve (find relevant content via an index), Augment (combine question + grounding data into a prompt), Generate (model outputs a grounded answer with possible citations).
- Retrieval modes: keyword, semantic, vector, and hybrid search; Azure AI Search is recommended for RAG in Foundry.
- Agentic RAG: an advanced pattern where a model generates subqueries to fetch focused grounding data in parallel, improving handling of complex inputs.
- Practical note: RAG is most effective when retrieval is fast and reliable, enabling grounded responses and source citations.

Summary:
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is an architecture that enhances AI model performance by connecting a generative model with external knowledge bases. It combines an information retrieval component with a generator to produce more accurate, domain-specific content without retraining the model. Key roles:
- Knowledge base: external data source (internal docs, journals, specialized datasets)
- Retriever: converts the user query into embeddings and fetches relevant data from the knowledge base
- Integration layer: coordinates retrieval and generation, creating an augmented prompt (original query + retrieved context)
- Generator: produces the final output using the augmented prompt (often pretrained models like GPT, Claude, or Llama)

2) The integration layer combines the retrieved data with the original query to form an augmented prompt.

citations.title: Do We Still Need GraphRAG? Benchmarking RAG and GraphRAG for Agentic Search Systems
citations.excerpt:
Summary:
- This work introduces RAGSearch, a unified benchmark for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) under agentic (multi-round, decision-based) search workflows.
- It compares dense RAG and graph-based RAG (GraphRAG) as alternative retrieval infrastructures within the RAG paradigm, across training-free and training-based agentic inference.
- Key goal: assess whether agentic search can compensate for the lack of explicit graph structure, reducing the need for GraphRAG in complex reasoning tasks.
- Methodology highlights:
  - Standardized LLM backbone, retrieval budgets, and inference protocols
  - Full test-set evaluation with both offline preprocessing costs and online inference efficiency included
  - Evaluates across multiple QA benchmarks in iterative, multi-step settings
- Findings:
  - Agentic search substantially improves dense RAG performance and narrows the gap to GraphRAG, especially in reinforcement-learning–based (RL-based) agentic setups
  - GraphRAG still offers advantages for complex multi-hop reasoning and yields more stable agentic behavior when its offline costs are amortized
- Practical takeaway: explicit graph structure and agentic search play complementary roles; design choices should consider task complexity (multi-hop vs. simpler QA) and cost trade-offs.
- Resources: benchmark and code available at GitHub (RAGSearch).

The paper benchmarks how much reasoning retrieval-augmented models (RAG) gain beyond base LLMs by introducing HybridRAG-Bench, a fully automated framework for evaluating multi-hop reasoning over hybrid knowledge (text and structured graphs). Key points:
- Framework purpose: quantify additional reasoning contributed by retrieval-augmented approaches that combine unstructured text with structured knowledge graphs.
- Pipeline: four stages

  2) Build hybrid knowledge environments with aligned unstructured text chunks and knowledge graphs to support both document retrieval and graph traversal.
  3) Generate diverse QA pairs grounded in explicit reasoning paths (single-hop, multi-hop, hard multi-hop, conditional, counterfactual, open-ended).
  4) Automated quality control to ensure answerability, independence from document phrasing, and non-redundancy.

citations.title: MIRAGE: A Metric-Intensive Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
citations.excerpt:
Summary:
MIRAGE is a compact, high-signal benchmark designed to evaluate Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. It presents 7,560 QA queries linked to a retrieval pool of 37,800 document chunks, with at least one positive chunk per query and several challenging negatives. This structure enables precise, fast evaluation of both retrieval and generation components, while keeping the retrieval pool manageable. The authors introduce four new metrics to analyze RAG behavior: noise vulnerability, context acceptability, context insensitivity, and context misinterpretation, capturing how retrieval and generation interact under varying input conditions. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available for easy integration and customization.

citations.title: Open-Source Agentic Hybrid RAG Framework for Scientific Literature Review
citations.excerpt:
Summary:
- Objective: Presents an open-source, agentic hybrid Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for scientific literature review that dynamically selects between graph-based (GraphRAG) and vector-based (VectorRAG) retrieval, with uncertainty quantification.
- Key components:
  - Data ingestion from PubMed, arXiv, and Google Scholar APIs to build a Neo4j knowledge graph with citation relationships.
  - Full-text PDFs embedded into a FAISS vector store using all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
  - A Llama-3.3-70B versatile agent that decides per query whether GraphRAG or VectorRAG is most appropriate, and adjusts instruction-tuned generation accordingly.
  - Uncertainty estimates provided at runtime to improve transparency and reduce hallucinations.
- Retrieval and reasoning:
  - GraphRAG: translates user queries into Cypher queries over the KG.
  - VectorRAG: combines sparse and dense retrieval with re-ranking over the embedding space.
- Evaluation:
  - Bootstrapped with 12 resamples; uncertainty quantified via standard deviations.
  - Instruction-Tuned Agent with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) outperforms baselines.
  - Reported gains (vs baseline) include improvements in VS Context Recall (+0.63), Context Precision (+0.56), Faithfulness (+0.24), KG Answer Relevance (+0.12), and overall Precision (+0.04–0.11 range across metrics).
- Significance: Demonstrates improved relevance, reduced hallucinations, and reproducible workflows by dynamically selecting retrieval pathways and integrating uncertainty, contributing to robust, scalable autonomous literature discovery.

Summary:
- Objective: Presents an open-source, agentic hybrid Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for scientific literature review that dynamically selects between graph-based (GraphRAG) and vector-based (VectorRAG) retrieval, with uncertainty quantification.
- Key components:
  - Data ingestion from PubMed, arXiv, and Google Scholar APIs to build a Neo4j knowledge graph with citation relationships.
  - Full-text PDFs embedded into a FAISS vector store using all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
  - A Llama-3.3-70B versatile agent that decides per query whether GraphRAG or VectorRAG is most appropriate, and adjusts instruction-tuned generation accordingly.
  - Uncertainty estimates provided at runtime to improve transparency and reduce hallucinations.
- Retrieval and reasoning:
  - GraphRAG: translates user queries into Cypher queries over the KG.
  - VectorRAG: combines sparse and dense retrieval with re-ranking over the embedding space.
- Evaluation:
  - Bootstrapped with 12 resamples; uncertainty quantified via standard deviations.
  - Instruction-Tuned Agent with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) outperforms baselines.
  - Reported gains (vs baseline) include improvements in VS Context Recall (+0.63), Context Precision (+0.56), Faithfulness (+0.24), KG Answer Relevance (+0.12), and overall Precision (+0.04–0.11 range across metrics).
- Significance: Demonstrates improved relevance, reduced hallucinations, and reproducible workflows by dynamically selecting retrieval pathways and integrating uncertainty, contributing to robust, scalable autonomous literature discovery.
